new_statements.quote: p. 4: "[r] and [d] probably do not contrast. [r] is medial before an unstressed vowel (e.g. mārē 'woman'), [d] is initial, and medial before a stressed vowel (e.g. páádòì 'lizard')." p. 6: "the present tense (or perhaps more accurately, the participial) suffix -rá, which normally drops its initial consonant when it is preceded by a stressed vowel, as is the case when it is added to a monosyllabic verb root: pó-á 'going out'; tí-á 'pounding'." p. 9: "There are four tone levels in Jɔ. Although most Mande languages have two tone levels, four-level systems are not unknown"
new_statements.citation: Carlson, Robert. 1993. A sketch of Jɔ: A Mande language with a feminine pronoun. Mandenkan 25: 1-109.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (113 pp., image-only; scanned in scanned/; printed page = PDF page - 4). I rendered PDF pages 8, 10, 13 (printed pp. 4, 6, 9) and read them against the scanned. All three quoted passages are there verbatim: p. 4, §2.1, second paragraph after Figure 1: "[r] and [d] probably do not contrast. [r] is medial before an unstressed vowel (e.g. mārē 'woman'), [d] is initial, and medial before a stressed vowel (e.g. páádòì 'lizard')."; p. 6, §2.1, third paragraph: "The other tense-aspect suffix which can create vowel clusters is the present tense (or perhaps more accurately, the participial) suffix -rá, which normally drops its initial consonant when it is preceded by a stressed vowel,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jɔ/Jowulu is described as a tone language with four level tones (T, H, M, L) plus glides; Carlson never states where word stress falls. 'Stressed'/'unstressed vowel' appears only as a conditioning environment for [r]~[d] allophony, for vowel elision yielding kl/kr/bl clusters, and for [r]-drop of the suffix -rá after monosyllabic verb roots. The examples do not yield a consistent position (mārē: second vowel unstressed; páádòì: vowel after medial d stressed), and Carlson states the phonology 'remains to be worked out' (p. 3).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the stress notion itself is undefined.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from elicited citation forms and a 1991 field word list (Siranikoroba/Koura, Mali); stress is not part of the transcription, only tone is marked.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Carlson 1993 describes 'Jɔ' (jowulu) of the arrondissement of Loulouni south of Sikasso, Mali (informant from Siranikoroba, plus Koura) = jowu1238; he identifies Prost's 1958 'Don' (Téna, Burkina Faso) as the same language. Note the tone-count discrepancy: Carlson posits four tone levels, whereas Kim 2003 (SIL) marks three and McPherson 2020 (following Djilla et al. 2004) calls Jowulu a three-tone language. 'Samogho' is a cover term also used for the unrelated-within-Mande Duun/Dzùùngoo (Samogohiri) and Seenku; the Köppe/Solomiac 'dzùùngoo de Samogohiri' volumes are NOT Jowulu.

sources.note: §2 'Some phonological characteristics' (pp. 3-12): 'the phonology of Jɔ remains to be worked out'; §2.3 Tone (p. 9): four tone levels T/H/M/L, tone triplets and pairs given. No statement of where stress falls; 'stressed'/'unstressed vowel' is used only as a conditioning environment on pp. 4, 5, 6 ([r] medial before an unstressed vowel vs [d] before a stressed vowel; clusters kl/kr/bl from elision of an unstressed vowel; suffix -rá drops its [r] after a stressed vowel = after a monosyllabic verb root). Pages 1-60 scanned and grepped; pp. 61-113 (word list) not scanned.
